inclusion_rule: Studies whose ledger text names decoding, classification or recognition together with imagined, covert, inner or unspoken speech (any signal: EEG, MEG, ECoG, sEEG, intracortical, EMG, video). The design of interest is a decoder trained and tested on imagined-speech trials, with an overt condition on the same items in the same participants, from intracranial recordings. Boundary: attempted speech by paralysed users is a different action and is not counted as imagined speech; the ledger pattern also admits lip-reading and perception studies that mention covert speech, so counts are upper bounds; versions of one study count once; usual approach judged on studies first public before 2011.

usual_approach.note_triage: Triage 2026-11-26: the 39 prior pattern-match hits are mostly audiovisual, lip-reading and phonetics papers. Among them the only imagined-speech decoder is Deng 2010 (EEG, imagined syllable rhythm, no overt condition). Guenther 2009 (intracortical, attempted speech) was missed by the pattern and read separately. No clean design count over imagined-speech decoders before 2011 is large enough to state; the review table shows no count for M04 (matched null).

read_fulltext.quote: In the current study we use a novel approach to speech restoration in which we decode continuous auditory parameters for a real-time speech synthesizer from neuronal activity in motor cortex during attempted speech.
High density EEG data were recorded for seven subjects while they produced in imagination one of two syllables in one of three different rhythms.
Researchers verbally instructed the patient to articulate a word multiple times, with approximately one-second intervals between repetitions.

This screening procedure began with an experiment in which ECoG signals were recorded while the subject either overtly (patient 1, 2, and 3) or covertly (patient 3 and 4) expressed a series of four phonemes
We further developed a generalized decoding framework that achieved high prediction accuracy for speech imagery (median 80.4%; chance 16.7%), comparable to speech articulation (78.3%).
The most important finding here is that standard classification techniques can be reasonably applied to the problem of predicting attempted productions of phonemes from neural activity
